vesugen.summary: A three-amino-acid peptide (KED) people use hoping for healthier blood vessels and a fresher, younger-looking complexion.

quick.overview:
Vesugen is a short peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) from Vladimir Khavinson's bioregulator program, described as a vascular-support peptide. People take it hoping that healthier circulation shows up as fresher, younger-looking skin.

The chain runs from vessel health to circulation to skin tone. Published work is mostly in cell cultures, where it was reported to restore the proliferation marker Ki-67 in aged vascular cells and to limit lipid peroxidation of lipoproteins. One small Russian human report exists; skin or appearance has not been measured.
quick.how: Users treat it as part of a broader anti-aging peptide routine, often alongside other Khavinson bioregulators, taken in periodic courses rather than continuously. Users generally report looking for gradual, general changes over weeks to months rather than a specific visible result.
quick.risks: There is no systematic human safety data. It is not an approved medicine and is sold as a research peptide, so product quality varies and legal status depends on the country.

angle.text: Longevity users take Vesugen as a vascular peptide, hoping better blood vessel health translates into fresher, younger-looking skin. Cell-culture studies report effects on aged vascular cells; the skin-appearance link is a theory users draw.

crystagen.summary: A three-amino-acid Khavinson peptide taken for spleen and immune support as part of broader anti-aging stacks.

quick.overview:
Crystagen (Thr-Lys-Glu) is a short peptide from the Khavinson family of bioregulators, described as an immune-supporting peptide for the ageing spleen. Users add it to anti-aging routines hoping a healthier immune profile contributes to ageing well overall.

The chain runs from spleen and immune function to a healthier ageing profile. A 2014 Russian gerontology paper reported that it activates B-cells in the spleen of ageing animals, alongside related peptides. The literature is small and mostly from the developing group; no human trial was found.
quick.how: It is used in periodic courses within multi-peptide longevity routines, often next to other Khavinson peptides. Users generally expect slow, general effects rather than a specific visible change.
quick.risks: No human safety data was found. It is sold as a research peptide rather than an approved medicine, so purity and legal status vary by country.

angle.text: Crystagen is used in peptide-bioregulator circles as a spleen and immune peptide, folded into anti-aging stacks in the hope of healthier ageing overall. Animal and lab reports describe B-cell activation in the ageing spleen; appearance has not been studied.

chonluten.summary: A three-amino-acid Khavinson peptide associated with airway lining health and general wellbeing.

quick.overview:
Chonluten (Glu-Asp-Gly) is a short peptide from the Khavinson bioregulator family, associated with the mucosal lining of the airways. People use it for respiratory and general health rather than for a particular look.

The chain runs from support of airway mucosa to easier breathing to better general health. A 2022 cell-line study tested it with other Khavinson peptides for effects on proliferation and inflammatory pathways in cultured monocyte/macrophage cells. No human trial was found.
quick.how: It is taken in periodic courses within peptide-bioregulator routines, often alongside other Khavinson peptides. Users generally describe it as a background health addition with no specific timeline.
quick.risks: No human safety data was found. It is sold as a research peptide rather than an approved medicine, so quality and legal status vary.

angle.text: Chonluten is promoted in peptide-bioregulator communities as an airway and lung mucosa peptide, used for respiratory and general health rather than a specific look. It has been tested in cultured immune cells; no appearance use has been studied.

livagen.summary: A four-amino-acid Khavinson peptide used by anti-aging enthusiasts hoping cells, and eventually looks, stay younger.

quick.overview:
Livagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala) is a short peptide from Khavinson's group in Russia, described as a regulator of gene activity in ageing cells. Forum users pitch it as a non-injectable-style anti-aging option meant to keep cells acting younger and, in turn, looking younger.

The chain runs from chromatin and gene-expression effects to cells behaving younger to a younger appearance. Researchers report that it loosens condensed heterochromatin and activates ribosomal genes in lymphocytes from older donors, and stimulates liver tissue growth in culture. Studies are small and mostly in cell cultures and rats; skin, hair and bone have not been tested in people.
quick.how: It is used in periodic courses as part of broader longevity stacks, often with other bioregulator peptides. Users describe expecting slow, cumulative effects over months.
quick.risks: No human safety data was found. It is sold online as a research peptide rather than an approved medicine, so product purity and legal status vary by country.

angle.text: Livagen is pitched by forum users as a peptide that makes cells act younger, which they hope shows up as younger-looking skin, hair and tissue. Lab work reports chromatin changes in cells from older donors; visible ageing has not been tested in people.

thymalin.summary: A Russian calf-thymus peptide extract used for immune support and as a general anti-aging option.

quick.overview:
Thymalin is a calf-thymus extract developed in Russia as an immune-modulating drug and promoted within the Khavinson family of bioregulator peptides for ageing. Looksmaxxing interest is a general hope that a healthier immune system supports ageing well.

The chain runs from thymic peptides to immune modulation to a healthier ageing profile. Proponents say its peptides support T-cell differentiation; the dipeptide Thymogen and the synthetic Vilon were derived from it. Support comes mostly from animal studies and reports by its developers.
quick.how: It is used in periodic courses, usually in Russian-style bioregulator protocols or alongside other longevity peptides. Users generally expect general, gradual effects rather than a visible change.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed do not describe human adverse effects. It is an animal-derived preparation, and legal status varies by country.

angle.text: Thymalin is a calf-thymus extract used in Russia as an immune drug and taken by longevity enthusiasts hoping for healthier ageing. Data comes mostly from its developers; appearance outcomes have not been measured.

epithalamin.summary: The bovine pineal extract behind Epitalon, used by longevity enthusiasts hoping to slow ageing, including how old they look.

quick.overview:
Epithalamin is a pineal-gland peptide extract developed in Russia by Khavinson's group, from which the tetrapeptide Epitalon was derived. Longevity enthusiasts use it hoping to slow ageing, including how old they look.

The chain runs from pineal peptides to melatonin and rhythm effects to slower visible ageing. The developing group reports longer lifespan in flies, mice and rats, and raised melatonin production in old rats. No randomized human trial was found.
quick.how: It is used in periodic courses within longevity routines, often discussed alongside Epitalon. Users generally describe long-horizon, general aims rather than quick visible results.
quick.risks: Human safety data was not found in the sources reviewed. It is an animal-derived preparation not approved in most countries.

angle.text: Epithalamin, the pineal extract behind Epitalon, is used by longevity enthusiasts hoping to slow ageing, including how old someone looks. Lifespan and melatonin effects are reported in animals; appearance has not been measured in people.

cortexin.summary: A Russian cattle-brain peptide medicine used for neurological conditions and discussed as a nootropic.

quick.overview:
Cortexin is a peptide complex made from cattle brain cortex and prescribed in Russia and nearby countries for neurological conditions. Biohackers list it as a nootropic-style option for cognition and general wellbeing; it is not a cosmetic product.

The chain runs from a neuroprotective peptide mixture to neurological support to cognition and wellbeing. A rat study found protective effects in brain ischemia models, and a Russian randomized study looked at chronic cerebral ischemia. No appearance use is documented.
quick.how: In Russia it is given as a prescribed course of injections for neurological conditions. Outside that setting, it appears in biohacking lists as a periodic course.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed give limited safety information. It is an animal-derived injectable available by prescription in Russia and not approved in most countries.

angle.text: Cortexin is a cattle-brain peptide medicine used mainly in Russia for neurological conditions and listed by biohackers as a nootropic-style option. Local trials address neurology; appearance has not been studied.

retinalamin.summary: An animal-derived retinal peptide extract from Russia, used for eye conditions and discussed in longevity circles for eye health.

quick.overview:
Retinalamin is a peptide extract made from animal retinas, developed in Russia in Khavinson's group. It is used there, mostly by injection, for glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy, and longevity enthusiasts list it for eye health. It is not a cosmetic product.

The chain runs from a retinal peptide complex to support of retinal cells to eye health. Russian-language studies report improvements in some structural and functional measures in people with glaucoma compared with controls, and cell work reports stimulated proliferation of retinal and pigment epithelial cells. No cosmetic eye use is documented.
quick.how: In clinical use it is given as courses of injections alongside standard eye care. In longevity circles it is listed next to other Khavinson preparations.
quick.risks: Published safety data come mainly from Russian studies by the developer's network. It is not approved as a drug in most Western countries, and independent Western trials are not documented.

angle.text: Retinalamin is an animal-derived retinal peptide used clinically in Russia for glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy, and discussed in longevity circles for eye health. It has been studied for those retinal conditions; no cosmetic eye use is documented.

prostatilen.summary: A cattle prostate peptide extract used in post-Soviet urology and listed in longevity circles for general health.

quick.overview:
Prostatilen is a peptide extract from cattle prostate, developed in the Soviet Union and used in Russia and nearby countries for prostatitis and prostate enlargement. Longevity circles list it with other Khavinson bioregulators as a general-health option. It is a urology product, not a cosmetic one.

The chain runs from a tissue-specific prostate extract to urological support to general health. Early-1990s Russian reports looked at prostatitis, rat studies report changes in prostate size and oxidative-stress markers, and a 2026 paper examined prostate-derived peptide preparations and erectile function in men with chronic prostatitis.
quick.how: Clinically it is given in courses for prostate conditions in post-Soviet countries. In longevity circles it appears alongside other bioregulator peptides.
quick.risks: Safety information comes mostly from regional studies; two older mouse studies examined mutagenicity. It is not a Western-approved drug, and independent trials are not documented.

angle.text: Prostatilen is a bovine prostate extract used in post-Soviet urology for prostatitis and enlargement, and mentioned in bioregulator discussions as a general-health option. Data is mostly Russian-language clinical work; no appearance use is described.

cortagen.summary: A Khavinson brain-derived tetrapeptide (AEDP) used by longevity enthusiasts for neural ageing and cognition.

quick.overview:
Cortagen (Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro) is a four-amino-acid peptide made by Khavinson's group, modelled on the brain-cortex preparation Cortexin. Interest is in cognition and brain ageing rather than looks.

The chain runs from a brain-tissue peptide to support of neural ageing to cognitive wellbeing. Studies cover cell cultures, rodents and small reports, with changes in gene and interleukin-2 expression, sciatic nerve regeneration and free-radical processes. One Russian report compared Cortexin and Cortagen in chronic ischaemia.
quick.how: It is used in periodic courses within longevity peptide routines, often with other Khavinson peptides. Users describe expecting slow, general effects.
quick.risks: Human safety data are essentially absent from the published literature, and it is not an approved drug in Western countries.

angle.text: Cortagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide modelled on Cortexin, used by longevity enthusiasts for brain ageing and cognition. It has been studied in cells and animals; appearance has not been studied.

ovagen.summary: A Khavinson liver-targeted tripeptide (EDL) listed in longevity circles for liver and gut support.

quick.overview:
Ovagen (Glu-Asp-Leu) is a three-amino-acid peptide developed by Khavinson's group in Russia and described as acting on the liver and digestive tract. Longevity lists mention it for organ support, not for a particular look.

The chain runs from a liver-targeted peptide to tissue-specific gene-expression changes to liver and gut health. Its developers propose that short peptides bind DNA and regulate gene expression. Verified published studies on it are scarce, mostly from Russian institutions.
quick.how: It is used in periodic courses in bioregulator routines, often alongside other Khavinson peptides.
quick.risks: No human safety data could be verified. It is sold as a research compound or supplement and is not an approved drug in most countries.

angle.text: Ovagen is a Khavinson tripeptide described as acting on the liver and digestive tract, mentioned in longevity lists for organ support. Published human data is thin; no appearance use is described.

pancragen.summary: A Khavinson pancreas-targeted tetrapeptide used for metabolic and ageing support.

quick.overview:
Pancragen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp) is a four-amino-acid peptide from Khavinson's group in Saint Petersburg, designed to target pancreatic tissue. Bioregulator users take it for metabolic and ageing support, not for a particular look.

The chain runs from pancreas-targeted effects to metabolic support to healthier metabolism. It raised expression of differentiation factors in pancreatic cell cultures, and has been studied in diabetic rats and aged rhesus monkeys. One small study in older people reported lower fasting glucose and insulin resistance index in treated patients. Nearly all work comes from the developing group.
quick.how: It is used in periodic courses within longevity routines, often alongside other bioregulator peptides.
quick.risks: Human safety data are very limited, and it is not an approved drug in Western countries.

angle.text: Pancragen is a Khavinson tetrapeptide designed to target pancreatic tissue, used in bioregulator circles for metabolic and ageing support. A small human study reported lower fasting glucose; appearance has not been measured.

prostamax.summary: A four-amino-acid Khavinson peptide modelled on prostate extract and used for prostate support in longevity circles.

quick.overview:
Prostamax (Lys-Glu-Asp-Pro) is a short peptide from Khavinson's group in St. Petersburg, designed around the composition of the prostate extract Prostatilen. People in longevity and research-peptide circles use it for prostate support and general health.

The chain runs from a prostate-targeted peptide to prostate tissue support to general health. Published work consists of cell-culture and rat-tissue experiments, plus in vitro studies in lymphocytes from elderly donors reporting effects on chromatin structure. No human trials were found.
quick.how: It is used in periodic courses within bioregulator routines, often alongside peptides such as Epitalon.
quick.risks: No human safety data from trials were found. It has no regulatory approval for human use and is sold as a research chemical, so product purity is not assured.

angle.text: Prostamax is a Khavinson tetrapeptide modelled on the prostate extract Prostatilen and used for prostate support in longevity communities. Evidence is cell and rat-tissue work; no appearance use is described.

testagen.summary: A four-amino-acid bioregulator peptide promoted for testosterone support, which users link to a leaner, more muscular look.

quick.overview:
Testagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Gly) is a short peptide in the Khavinson bioregulator family, promoted in research-peptide and longevity communities for testicular function and testosterone. Users link higher testosterone to muscle, leanness and masculine features.

The chain runs from testicular support to higher testosterone to a leaner, more muscular look. Published work shows that labelled short peptides including Testagen can enter cultured cells and nuclei, and a 2025 materials paper studied it as a copper-corrosion inhibitor. No studies in people were found.
quick.how: It is used in periodic courses in research-peptide routines, sometimes alongside other hormone-support approaches.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found. It is not an approved medicine and is sold unregulated as a research chemical.

angle.text: Testagen is promoted in research-peptide communities as supporting testicular function and testosterone, which users link to muscle, leanness and masculine features. The claim comes from developer material; no human studies have been published.

thymulin.summary: A zinc-dependent thymus hormone discussed in peptide and zinc circles for immune and general health.

quick.overview:
Thymulin is a nine-amino-acid hormone made by the thymus that needs zinc to be active. It appears in peptide and zinc discussions as an immune and general-health option, not as a cosmetic one.

The chain runs from a zinc-dependent thymic hormone to immune regulation to general health. It was described by Jean-Francois Bach and colleagues in 1977 and has been studied for T-cell differentiation, neuroendocrine regulation and inflammation. Human data cover zinc status and thymic function, not supplement use.
quick.how: Some vendors sell it as a research peptide in longevity circles; users often pair the idea with attention to zinc intake.
quick.risks: No human safety trials of the peptide were found. It is not an approved drug and is sold unregulated.

angle.text: Thymulin is a thymus hormone that needs zinc to be active, discussed in peptide and zinc circles for immune and general health. Human data covers zinc status and thymic function; appearance has not been studied.

thymosin-beta-4.summary: A natural repair peptide sold as TB-500, used for tissue recovery and by hair-loss hobbyists hoping for follicle effects; banned in sport.

quick.overview:
Thymosin beta-4 is a naturally occurring 43-amino-acid peptide that regulates actin inside cells. Sold as TB-500, lifters use it hoping to recover faster from tissue injuries, and hair-loss hobbyists hope for effects on follicles.

The chain runs from actin binding to cell migration, new blood vessels and tissue repair to faster recovery and possibly hair growth. Phase 2 trials tested it in skin ulcers, epidermolysis bullosa, dry eye and corneal wounds, with mixed or incomplete results reported. Hair findings come from mouse studies.
quick.how: It circulates online as a research peptide, along with the TB-500 fragment, and is used in periodic courses by people in recovery and hair-loss communities.
quick.risks: Trials reported mild effects, but long-term data are lacking. Its blood-vessel-promoting activity raises theoretical tumor concerns. It is unapproved, prohibited by WADA, and gray-market products vary in purity.

angle.text: Sold as TB-500, thymosin beta-4 is used by lifters for tissue recovery and by hair-loss hobbyists hoping for follicle effects. Human trials cover wounds and eyes; hair data is from mice.

thymosin-fraction-5.summary: The calf-thymus extract that thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 were purified from, relevant mainly as their source.

quick.overview:
Thymosin fraction 5 is a calf-thymus extract made in 1972 by Allan Goldstein's group, containing dozens of peptides. Thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 were later purified from it. It matters to this wiki as the origin of peptides that people use for recovery and healthier ageing.

The extract restored immune function in thymus-deficient animals, which led to the idea of thymic hormones. Clinical work focuses on purified thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) in infection and cancer, not on the extract for appearance.
quick.how: It is rarely used directly; people in thymic-peptide discussions generally use the purified peptides instead.
quick.risks: No approved use of the extract was found, and no appearance-related safety data. Animal-derived mixtures vary in composition.

angle.text: Thymosin fraction 5 is the calf-thymus extract from which thymosin alpha-1 and beta-4 were purified. It shows up in thymic-peptide discussions as the source of those peptides; no appearance use is documented.

thymopentin.summary: A thymus-derived immune peptide studied for infections and skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis.

quick.overview:
Thymopentin is a five-amino-acid peptide (arginine, lysine, aspartate, valine, tyrosine) based on the thymus hormone thymopoietin and classed as an immunostimulant. Interest for looks comes from its use in skin conditions: calmer skin when inflammatory disease is involved.

The chain runs from a thymus-derived peptide to changes in T-cell activity to calmer skin in inflammatory disease. It has been tested in HIV, atopic dermatitis, cancer and other immune-related conditions. No published trial has tested it for an appearance outcome.
quick.how: It is used in some countries as an immune drug; in peptide circles it is mentioned as an immune-modulating compound. Much recent work concerns delivery systems because peptides are poorly absorbed orally.
quick.risks: Safety information was not covered in the sources reviewed. Its regulatory status varies by country, and it is not an approved appearance treatment.

angle.text: Thymopentin is an immune peptide used in some countries for infections and studied in skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis and eczema, where the hoped-for payoff is calmer skin. Trials on cosmetic outcomes have not been reported.

ghrp-3.summary: A growth hormone-releasing peptide discussed by physique enthusiasts for GH-driven muscle and leanness.

quick.overview:
GHRP-3 is one of a numbered family of synthetic peptides that stimulate growth hormone release. Physique enthusiasts discuss it as a way to raise GH and IGF-1 for more muscle and less fat.

The chain runs from growth hormone release to higher GH and IGF-1 to more muscle and leanness. Like other GHRPs, it is classed as an agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor. Published work on it is mostly analytical chemistry for doping control; no completed human trial was found.
quick.how: It is used in research-peptide routines in physique communities, usually alongside training and diet. It is much less documented than better-known secretagogues.
quick.risks: No safety data from human trials were found. It is named on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list and is not an approved medicine.

angle.text: GHRP-3 is one of the numbered growth hormone-releasing peptides, discussed by physique enthusiasts as a way to raise GH for muscle and leanness. It is mostly known from anti-doping literature; human training or appearance trials have not been reported.

ghrp-4.summary: An obscure growth hormone-releasing peptide mentioned in physique forums for GH-driven muscle and fat loss.

quick.overview:
GHRP-4 belongs to a family of synthetic peptides designed to prompt growth hormone release. Physique forums mention it next to better-known secretagogues as a way to raise GH for muscle and fat loss.

The chain runs from growth hormone release to higher GH and IGF-1 to more muscle and leanness. It is classed as an agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor and is described as a met-enkephalin analogue. The published record consists of doping-control chemistry; no human clinical studies were found.
quick.how: It is used in research-peptide routines in physique communities, usually alongside training and diet, and is far less documented than other GHRPs.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found. It appears on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list and is not an approved medicine.

angle.text: GHRP-4 is an obscure member of the GHRP series that physique forums mention alongside better-known secretagogues for GH-driven muscle and fat loss. It appears in anti-doping analytical papers; human trials have not been reported.
